system.name: Jetpack
system.one_liner: a consensus system that makes fast-path commitment (CURP) generally safe when layered atop Raft

content.subject: how two view-change gaps in CURP+Raft let conflicting commands A and B silently violate fast-commit durability or ordering

relations.what: a client submits a command directly to whichever server is currently believed to be the leader
getRecoveryData from the new leader freezes and collects state from every witness during a view change
end & start messages reset witness state after recovery completes
the leader replicates its Raft log entries to the other replicas

panels.label: Case 1
panels.differs: a gap related to R1: a fast-committed command A can be silently lost when a stale witness (S1) later clears its state during a delayed recovery, letting a new leader (S3) insert command B in its place

panels.label: Case 2
panels.differs: a gap related to R2: after S1 recovers and is re-elected, it appends recovered command B after its own uncommitted command A and commits both, breaking the promised commit order from the previous term

content.key_idea: Two lettered replay scenarios show how CURP+Raft's view-change recovery can either silently drop a fast-committed command (Case 1) or let a recovered leader commit two conflicting commands out of their promised order (Case 2).
content.reading_order: Left to right through Case 1's six lettered frames (a-f) on top, tracking server rows S1-S5 and their witness/log state and term; then through Case 2's four frames (a-d) below.

palette.used_for: dark-grey text, server labels (S1-S5), and 'Term' captions
light-grey fill marking a crashed or stale replica's witness/log boxes

style.fill: flat, with crashed replicas shown in flat grey fill
style.stroke: thin black outlines on every witness circle and log square
style.arrows: colour-coded straight arrows for client requests, getRecoveryData, end & start, and replication messages
style.font: serif (Times New Roman) body text with Helvetica Neue for some labels
style.icons: a small crown icon marking the current Raft leader; a small burst/explosion icon marking a replica crash

encoding.color_means: arrow colour names the message kind - black for client requests, red for getRecoveryData, blue for end & start, green for replication - while grey fill marks a crashed or stale-witness replica
encoding.line_style_means: all message arrows are solid; no dashed lines are used, so timing and order are conveyed by left-to-right frame position and by the crown/crash icons rather than by line style
encoding.state_means: each server's row is redrawn in every lettered frame with its witness (circle) and log (square) contents, term number, leader crown, and crash icon updated to show that server's state at that moment
encoding.marker_means: letters (a) through (f)/(d) order the frames in time; the crown marks the current leader and the burst icon marks a crash
encoding.emphasis: the crown and crash icons, plus the colour-coded arrows converging on one server, draw the eye to exactly which replica is acting (or failing) in each frame
reusable_patterns: a fixed 5-row server roster redrawn frame by frame with coloured message arrows and leader/crash icons updating state, repeated once per failure-case row
weaknesses: ten densely lettered frames with five server rows each pack in a great deal of state, so tracking one specific replica across the full sequence takes careful attention
the difference between a plain grey fill (stale) and a grey fill with a burst icon (crashed) is subtle at this figure's size

evidence: the new leader broadcasts getRecoveryData to all witnesses
the new leader can insert a different command B where A should appear.
replicas carrying stale commands are never eligible for election, preventing this case by construction

summary: Figure 6 walks through two view-change failure scenarios in CURP+Raft using a five-server roster (S1-S5) redrawn across lettered frames, each server shown as a witness circle plus a Raft-log square, with colour-coded arrows for client requests, getRecoveryData, end-and-start, and replication messages. Case 1 (a-f) shows how command A can be fast-committed by a superquorum that includes S1's stale witness, but when a delayed end-and-start message later clears S1's witness state during a view change to leader S5 and then S3, the new leader S3 inserts a different command B in A's place, permanently losing the already fast-committed A. Case 2 (a-d) shows leader S1 committing unacknowledged command A, crashing and recovering after S5 fast-commits B, then re-appending and committing both A and B in an order that violates the prior term's ordering guarantee.
